clue.text: Pressure to consume carbon-rich fuel

blocks.note: P is the standard abbreviation for pressure in physics
to consume food is to eat it

explanation.surface: Someone presses a stove or power plant into burning a dirty, carbon-heavy fuel.
explanation.definitionFit: Peat is partly decayed plant matter dug from bogs, dried and burnt as a smoky fuel high in carbon.

clue.text: Character shown in Somerset hospital

indicators.note: shown in means on display inside the following words, so the letters sit within them

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: Someone describes the particular spirit or atmosphere on display at a hospital in Somerset, an English county.
explanation.definitionFit: An ethos is the distinctive spirit, values and outlook of a person or community, much as one speaks of its character.

clue.text: Can adept somehow perform like Astaire?

indicators.note: somehow says the letters arrive by some unspecified route, so their order is not to be trusted

blocks.note: the two words supply the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A question about whether a skilled performer could manage to move like the famous Hollywood dancer.
explanation.walkthrough: Fred Astaire was the American film star celebrated for his dancing, including tap routines with metal-plated shoes.
explanation.definitionFit: Fred Astaire's screen musicals were full of rhythmic footwork with metal-tipped shoes, so moving as he did is tapping out steps.

clue.text: Face extraordinary skiers

indicators.note: extraordinary means out of the usual order, so the letters are put into a new arrangement

blocks.note: the six letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Someone is told to confront some remarkable people on the ski slopes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Face' reads as a verb, confront; it is the noun, and kisser is slang for the face or mouth.
explanation.definitionFit: Kisser is informal slang for the mouth or whole face, the part used for kissing.

clue.text: Better to enjoy an evening here?

definitions.text: Better to enjoy an evening here?

blocks.clueFragment: Better to enjoy an evening here?
blocks.note: surface reading: a suggestion that some place would be a superior spot for a night out
setter's reading: a better is one who bets, and this is the venue where gamblers spend their nights wagering

explanation.surface: A recommendation that one would have a nicer night out at some particular venue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Better' looks like the comparative of good; read it as bet-ter, someone placing wagers.
explanation.definitionFit: A gambling house with roulette wheels and card tables is where people who wager spend a night.

clue.text: To Greeks at first a Roman habit

indicators.note: at first points to the opening letter of the word it follows

blocks.note: taken as written
the initial letter of the word
taken as written

explanation.surface: A historical remark that something began with the Greeks before it became a Roman custom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Habit' looks like a custom, but here it is clothing, as a monk's or a rider's habit is.
explanation.definitionFit: The toga was the loose draped woollen garment worn by citizens of ancient Rome, so it is their characteristic dress.

clue.text: Film artists a Romanist riled

indicators.note: riled means stirred up, and stirred-up letters lose their order

blocks.note: the nine letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Some film-makers have annoyed a Roman Catholic or scholar of Rome.
explanation.definitionFit: Those who create cartoons and other moving pictures by drawing or modelling frame by frame are artists working in film.

clue.text: Revolutionary at large shown in Sun leader

indicators.note: something revolutionary turns over, so the letters are read in the opposite direction
shown in means displayed inside something else, which places one group within another

blocks.note: taken as written
L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large
taken as written; it is split to hold the other letters

explanation.surface: A rebel who escaped is reported in the Sun newspaper's editorial.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sun leader' looks like a newspaper editorial; the Sun is the word to split and 'leader' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A sultan is a Muslim sovereign or ruler, the head of a sultanate, so he is a leader.

clue.text: Bobby grabbing hot meat slice

indicators.note: grabbing means taking hold of something, so one word wraps round the other

blocks.note: a bobby is British slang for a police officer
H is the abbreviation for hot, as on taps

explanation.surface: A police officer seizes a hot slice of meat, perhaps from a stall.
explanation.walkthrough: A bobby is an everyday British word for a police officer, named after Sir Robert Peel.
explanation.definitionFit: A chop is a thick cut of pork or lamb, usually including a rib bone, cooked as one portion.

clue.text: Wretched Dicky spied and wired message

indicators.note: dicky is British slang for faulty or unsound, so the letters following it are in a broken order

blocks.note: the five letters to rearrange
a cable is a telegram, a message sent by wire

explanation.surface: A wretched man called Dicky snooped and then sent a telegram, like a shabby spy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dicky' looks like a name; it is British slang for shaky or unsound (a dicky heart).
explanation.definitionFit: Wretched in the sense of contemptible or vile matches despicable, deserving to be despised.

clue.text: Like one area in largest continent

blocks.note: as and like both mean in the manner of
I is the Roman numeral for one
A is the abbreviation for area

explanation.surface: Something is compared to a single region within the world's biggest landmass.
explanation.definitionFit: Asia covers about a third of the Earth's land and holds most of its people, the biggest of the seven continents.

clue.text: Vessel not exactly broad in the beam?

definitions.text: Vessel not exactly broad in the beam?

blocks.clueFragment: Vessel not exactly broad in the beam?
blocks.note: surface reading: a jar or person with slim hips, since broad in the beam is an idiom for wide-bottomed
setter's reading: a beam is a ship's width, and this craft built for canals is famously slim

explanation.surface: A sly remark that some container, or someone, is rather slender about the hips.
explanation.walkthrough: Broad in the beam is a joking idiom for wide-hipped; a ship's beam is literally its width. These British canal boats are about seven feet wide.
explanation.definitionFit: British canal craft are built under seven feet across to fit the locks, so a ship of this kind has a slim beam.

clue.text: Grass over lovely Cambridge Backs

indicators.note: backs are the rear ends of things, pointing to the final letter of each word

blocks.note: the closing letter of each of the three words

explanation.surface: Lawns spread over the beautiful Backs, the riverside college gardens in Cambridge.
explanation.walkthrough: The Backs are the lawns behind the Cambridge colleges along the river Cam, so 'Cambridge Backs' reads as a place name.
explanation.definitionFit: Rye is a cereal grass grown for grain and fodder; ryegrass is also a common lawn grass.

clue.text: Repeatedly exclude one cold and brutal

blocks.note: to bar is to exclude, and 'repeatedly' asks for it twice
I is the Roman numeral for one
C is the abbreviation for cold, as on taps

explanation.surface: Keeping one person out again and again, coldly, is described as cruel.
explanation.definitionFit: Barbaric describes savagely cruel and uncivilised behaviour, so it is a close synonym for vicious violence.

clue.text: V-sign changes?

blocks.note: taken as written
Aries, the ram, is one of the signs of the zodiac

explanation.surface: A question about whether a rude two-fingered gesture has ever been altered.
explanation.walkthrough: The V-sign is a rude British hand gesture; the hyphen hides that V and 'sign' work separately, with 'sign' meaning a star sign.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb, varies means alters or becomes different, the same sense as the verb changes.

clue.text: Who stops poacher in match? Goalie!

blocks.note: a match is a game of football
a goalie is a goalkeeper, often just called the keeper

explanation.surface: In a football match, who blocks the striker who lurks to steal goals? The goalkeeper, obviously.
explanation.walkthrough: In football a poacher is a striker who snatches goals close to the net, so the surface seems to answer itself.
explanation.definitionFit: A gamekeeper is employed on a country estate to protect game birds and animals and catch anyone hunting them illegally.

clue.text: Blue planet close to Mercury

indicators.note: close here is the end of a word, so only the last letter is wanted

blocks.note: Earth is our own planet
the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: Earth, the blue planet, lies near Mercury in the solar system.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blue planet' is a stock phrase for Earth, but 'Blue' is the definition and 'planet' alone gives the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Blue humour is rude or risqué, and earthy humour is similarly coarse and frank about bodily matters.

clue.text: Serving includes ram’s heart for taste

indicators.note: includes means holds within, so one word goes inside the other
the heart of a word is its centre, so only the middle letter is taken

blocks.note: a plate is a serving of food, a plateful
the central letter of the three-letter word ram

explanation.surface: A portion of food comes with lamb's or mutton's heart in it, to suit someone's taste.
explanation.definitionFit: Palate means a person's sense of taste and ability to judge flavours, as in a refined palate.

clue.text: Live with a rook: ferocious creature!

blocks.note: to be is to exist or live
taken as written
R is the chess notation for rook

explanation.surface: Sharing a home with a black crow-like bird turns out to be a fierce experience.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rook' looks like the bird; here it is the chess piece, abbreviated R.
explanation.definitionFit: A bear is a large, powerful wild animal that can be dangerous and savage when provoked.

clue.text: An Aberdonian say in Berkshire town

blocks.note: an and a are the same indefinite article
someone from Aberdeen is, for example, a Scot; 'say' marks the example

explanation.surface: A man from Aberdeen, perhaps, is found in a town in southern England.
explanation.walkthrough: Aberdeen is a city in Scotland; Berkshire is a county west of London.
explanation.definitionFit: Ascot is a town in the English county of Berkshire, famous for its racecourse and Royal Ascot meeting.

clue.text: Heroine recalled being beaten about at home

indicators.note: something beaten is knocked out of shape, so its letters are reworked
about means surrounding, so the reworked letters go round the other piece

blocks.note: the eight letters to rearrange
someone at home is in

explanation.surface: A heroine remembers being beaten in her own home, a grim domestic story.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Recalled' reads as remembered; it is the fodder for the rearranging.
explanation.definitionFit: Cinderella is the fairy-tale heroine who is mistreated by her stepfamily before marrying the prince.

clue.text: Gone numb

blocks.note: first meaning: departed from life, no longer living
second meaning: without feeling, as a limb goes when its circulation is cut off

explanation.definitionFit: The adjective covers both someone no longer living and a limb that has lost all sensation, as in a dead leg.

clue.text: People in Derby perhaps?

blocks.note: first meaning: a group of people sharing descent, an ethnic group
second meaning: the Derby is a famous horse contest, an example of a contest of speed

explanation.surface: A question about who lives in Derby, a city in the English Midlands.
explanation.walkthrough: Derby is a city, but the Derby is also a famous flat horse race at Epsom; 'perhaps' marks it as one example.
explanation.definitionFit: The noun covers both a people of common ancestry and a contest of speed such as the Epsom Derby.

clue.text: Ordered at Ship get some pasta

indicators.note: ordered means put into a fresh order, so the letters are arranged anew

blocks.note: the nine letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Diners who order at a pub called the Ship are served some pasta.
explanation.walkthrough: The Ship is a common British pub name; 'Ordered' looks like placing an order for food.
explanation.definitionFit: Spaghetti is a kind of long, thin, string-like Italian pasta, so it is one example of pasta.

clue.text: Italian coming into church gives quote

indicators.note: coming into means entering, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: CE is the Church of England
It is short for Italian vermouth, as in gin and it

explanation.surface: An Italian walks into a church and recites a quotation.
explanation.walkthrough: Gin and it is a British cocktail of gin with Italian vermouth, which is why Italian gives IT.
explanation.definitionFit: To cite is to quote a passage or mention a source as evidence or authority.
